_comment: AP Cybersecurity 4.3: find what a filesystem is willing to tell you.
MOVED FROM TOPIC 1.2 ON 2026-09-02, REPORTED BY A TEACHER
Jukka Rauhala said the lab claimed a connection to 1.2 he could not see.
He was right. This lab teaches file permissions: who can read what, and who
left it that way. CED 1.2 is Suspicious Website Logins, which is password
attack signs, weak authentication and password hygiene. No overlap.
It is filed at 4.3 Protecting Devices because that is the closest home in
Unit 4, NOT because 4.3 teaches permissions. Measured on the live pages:
none of 4.1, 4.3, 4.4 or 4.5 mentions permissions, chmod, access control or
file mode at all, and 4.2 says "access control" once. So permissions are
graded on the exam (free response Part C writes a chmod command, see
docs/cyber-exam-format.md) and taught in no lesson in the course. This lab
is the only asset that teaches them. Moving it fixes a wrong label; it does
not close that gap.
item_id stays "1.2-lab" deliberately. It is an opaque key, referenced by the
live page mount, scripts/lab-pages-csv.js, scripts/page-availability.js and
two smoke suites. Renaming it buys a student nothing and breaks four things.
page_handle also stays: renaming a live handle is a human action.
WHY THIS ONE IS graded:false
scripts/seed-manifest.js deliberately does not seed ap-cybersecurity: that
course carries its own denominators (course_denominators and
course_unit_denominators, see docs/cyber-denominator-gaps.md). A lone
manifest row here would add points to every cyber student's denominator
through a second path, which is the exact failure smoke/manifest-prune.js
exists to prevent.
So this lab is playable and self-checking, and records nothing. Flipping it
to graded is this one field plus a seed run, once the cyber denominator
work in docs/cyber-denominator-gaps.md closes.
No em-dashes, per repo convention.
title: Find the tournament code
page_title: AP Cybersecurity Terminal Lab: Find the Tournament Code | Topic 4.3
seo_description: Hunt a file through a shared machine with nothing but a terminal, then work out who else could read it. Free AP Cybersecurity Topic 4.3 practice lab.
brief: The esports club is running a tournament after school and the join code is written down somewhere in the club's folders on the shared machine. Nobody remembers where.
You have a terminal and no file browser. That is the whole exercise: a filesystem will tell you what it holds if you ask it correctly.
1. `pwd` tells you where you are standing.
2. `ls` shows what is here. `ls -a` also shows the hidden entries.
3. `cd` moves you. `cd ..` moves you back up.
4. `cat` reads a file once you have found it.
5. When you are tired of guessing, `find . -name tournament_info.txt` searches for you.
Then answer the question below. Notice what else you could read on the way, and who left it readable.

questions.prompt: What is the tournament join code?
questions.explain: It is in clubs/esports/tournament/tournament_info.txt. The other three appear elsewhere on the machine, which is the point: a filesystem full of readable leftovers is a filesystem that leaks.

questions.prompt: On the way you could also read clubs/esports/roster_private.txt. What does that tell you about this machine?
options: Nothing, private files are always safe on a school machine
Any account that can reach the folder can read the roster, so the file is only as private as its permissions
The file is encrypted because it says private in the name
The roster cannot be read without a password
questions.explain: Naming a file private does nothing. Confidentiality comes from permissions and placement, not from the filename, and 'anyone who can open the folder can read it' is the default a lot of shared machines are left in.
